terms.definition: A file listing paths to leave out of the Docker build context, such as node_modules, .git, and .env.
A plain text file of NAME=value lines holding an app's settings and secrets. It is kept out of Git.
A backup rule of thumb: keep 3 copies of your data, on 2 different kinds of storage, with 1 copy off-site.
The HTTP status code meaning "your cached copy is still correct". It has no body, so it saves bandwidth.
The HTTP status code a server returns when a client has sent too many requests and must slow down.
The error a proxy returns when it couldn't get a valid response from the app behind it, often because the app is down.
The error a proxy returns when the app behind it took too long to respond.
A DNS record that maps a name to an IPv4 address.
A DNS record that maps a name to an IPv6 address.
A file location written from the root directory, like /var/log/nginx/error.log. It means the same thing from anywhere.
A specific way the app reads or writes data, such as "get a user's last 20 orders". Database design starts from these.
A short-lived token sent with API requests to prove the caller is allowed to make them.
The four guarantees of a database transaction: Atomicity (all or nothing), Consistency (rules hold), Isolation (concurrent work doesn't interfere), Durability (committed data survives crashes).
Automatic Certificate Management Environment: the standard protocol tools like Certbot use to request and renew certificates automatically.
Two ORM styles. In Active Record each object saves itself (user.save()); in Data Mapper plain objects are saved by a separate client or repository.
MongoDB's way of running multi-step queries, where documents pass through stages such as $match, $group, and $lookup (a join with another collection).
When so many alerts fire, mostly for nothing, that people start ignoring them, including the real ones.
The Prometheus component that receives fired alerts, groups them, and sends notifications to Slack, email, or a pager.
A routing method where the same IP address is announced from many locations, and the internet delivers each user to the nearest one.
The domain itself without any subdomain, like example.com instead of www.example.com. It cannot hold a CNAME record.
Application Programming Interface: a defined way for one program to ask another program for data or actions, like a menu of requests it accepts.
A long random secret given to a program so it can identify itself when calling an API.
Application performance monitoring: tools such as Datadog or New Relic that record each request's timing, including every database query it made.
A modern password hashing algorithm that is deliberately slow and needs lots of memory, making large-scale guessing expensive.
Cryptography with a key pair: a public key anyone may have and a private key only the owner holds. TLS uses it briefly, to agree on keys and prove identity.
JavaScript syntax built on promises: await pauses only the current async function until a promise settles, and errors can be caught with try/catch.
A delivery guarantee where every message arrives, but some may arrive more than once, so processing must handle duplicates.
A delivery guarantee where each message arrives once or not at all. Nothing is duplicated, but messages can be lost.
Access rules based on properties of the user, the data, and the situation, such as region, amount, or time of day.
Proving who you are, for example by logging in with a password, a passkey, or Google.
A kind of login evidence: something you know (a password), something you have (a phone or security key), or something you are (a fingerprint).
The DNS server that holds a domain's official records, usually run by your DNS provider.
Deciding what a known user is allowed to do, such as whether they may read a specific order.
A short-lived, one-time code from an OAuth provider that your server exchanges for tokens.
The default mode where each SQL statement runs as its own transaction and commits immediately.
One or more separate data centres inside a cloud region, with their own power and networking.
The default index structure: a balanced tree of sorted pages (root, branch, leaf) that finds any value in a few page reads, even in huge tables.
The part of an app that runs on servers: it stores data, applies business rules, and answers requests from the frontend.
Filling a new column or table with values for rows that already existed, usually in small batches on a live database.
Work a server does after it has already replied to the user, such as sending an email or processing a video, handled by a separate worker process.
How a slow destination tells a fast data source to pause, so unsent data does not pile up in memory.
How much data a connection can carry per second, like the width of a pipe.
A whole physical server rented or owned by one customer, with no virtualization shared with others.
A way to write any bytes as text using letters, digits, - and _, safe for URLs. It is an encoding, not encryption: anyone can decode it.
A server whose only job is to be the entry point into a private network. You SSH to it first, then hop onward to private machines.
An older, widely used slow password hashing algorithm with an adjustable cost. It only uses the first 72 bytes of a password.
A token that works for whoever holds it, like cash, with no further proof of identity.
An interview question about how you acted in a past situation, usually starting 'Tell me about a time...'.
The IP address a server listens on. 127.0.0.1 accepts connections only from the same machine; 0.0.0.0 accepts them on every network interface.
A specific folder or file from the host made visible inside a container. Both sides see the same files.
A plan step that first collects all matching row locations from an index, then reads each needed table page once, in page order.
Running the new version as a complete second environment and switching all traffic to it at once, keeping the old one ready for rollback.
A network of many hijacked computers controlled by an attacker, often used to spread attacks across thousands of IP addresses.
The one part of a system that limits the speed or capacity of everything else. Speeding up other parts doesn't help until it's fixed.
A private virtual network on one host that containers join. On user-defined bridge networks, containers find each other by name.
The app (Chrome, Safari, Firefox) that fetches web pages, runs their JavaScript, and draws them on screen.
Guessing a password by trying huge numbers of possibilities automatically.
The binary, JSON-like format MongoDB stores and sends. It adds types JSON lacks, such as dates, 64-bit integers, Decimal128, and ObjectId.
Docker's store of previously built layers. A layer is reused if its instruction and inputs are unchanged; the first change rebuilds every later layer.
The folder sent to Docker by docker build. COPY can only use files from it, and .dockerignore removes files from it.
A popular Node.js library for job queues that stores its data in Redis, with retries, delays, priorities, and schedules built in.
A saved copy of data kept somewhere faster to reach, so the same work does not have to be repeated.
Changing a file's URL when its content changes, usually by putting a hash of the content in the filename, so browsers and CDNs fetch the new version instead of an old cached copy.
The data you asked for was found in the cache, so the slower source was not needed.
Removing or replacing cached copies when the real data changes, so users stop seeing the old version.
The data was not in the cache, so it had to be fetched from the slower source.
When a popular cached value expires and many requests miss at the same moment, so they all hit the database for the same data at once.
A caching pattern where the app checks the cache first, and on a miss loads from the database and saves a copy in the cache.
An HTTP response header that tells browsers and CDNs whether they may store a response and for how long, using directives like max-age, no-cache, and no-store.
A function you pass to other code, so it can be called later, for example when a slow operation finishes.
Sending a small share of traffic to a new version first, watching its metrics, and increasing the share only if it looks healthy.
For metrics, the number of distinct time series a metric creates: one per unique combination of label values. High cardinality uses lots of memory.
Content Delivery Network: many servers around the world that keep copies of your files, so users download them from somewhere nearby.
A free program that gets certificates from Let's Encrypt, installs them into web servers like Nginx, and renews them automatically.
A file that proves a server owns a domain name. It is signed by a trusted organization so browsers can check it.
A trusted organisation that signs certificates, vouching that a server really owns a domain name.
A Linux kernel feature that limits what a group of processes can use, such as memory and CPU. Docker's --memory flag uses it.
The sequence of signatures from a site's certificate up through intermediate certificates to a root certificate authority the browser already trusts.
Reading a database's own change log to produce an event for every changed row, so other systems can react to every write.
The Linux command that changes a file's permissions, for example chmod 600 .env.
The Linux command that changes which user and group own a file, for example chown deploy:www-data file.
Automatically testing every change (CI), and building and releasing it the same way every time (CD).
A way to write a range of IP addresses, like 10.0.0.0/16. The number after the slash says how many leading bits are fixed; the rest can vary.
A safety switch in code that stops calling a failing service for a while after too many errors, then lets a few test requests through to see if it has recovered.
Loading a site in an invisible frame on another page and tricking the user into clicking buttons on it.
The program that sends a request and waits for an answer, such as a browser or a mobile app.
A password-like value that identifies your server to an OAuth provider. It must stay on the server.
The small difference between two machines' clocks, which time-based checks must tolerate.
A geographic area where a cloud provider has data centres, such as eu-west-1.
Running several copies of a Node app on one machine, sharing one port, so it can use every CPU core.
A DNS record that makes one name an alias of another name, so the resolver looks up the other name instead.
The extra delay when a serverless platform must create a fresh environment before running a function.
A step that undoes an earlier step in a saga, such as releasing reserved stock when payment fails.
An index on several columns, sorted by the first column, then the second within it. It helps queries that filter on its leading columns.
A request that asks the server to send the content only if it changed, using If-None-Match (with an ETag) or If-Modified-Since. If nothing changed, the answer is 304 Not Modified with no body.
TCP's way of slowing down when packets are lost, because loss usually means the network is overloaded.
Stopping new requests to an instance and letting in-flight ones finish before shutting it down.
A pooled connection that code checked out and never released, usually on an error path. Enough leaks empty the pool and requests start timing out.
A small set of open database connections that are reused, instead of opening a new one for every query.
A way of assigning keys to servers so that adding or removing a server moves only a small share of the keys instead of most of them.
A named set of consumers that share the messages of a stream or topic. Each message goes to one consumer in the group; different groups each get their own copy.
How far consumers are behind producers: the number of messages written but not yet processed. Growing lag means consumers can't keep up.
An app packaged with everything it needs, running isolated from other apps but sharing the host machine's operating system kernel.
A server that stores Docker images, such as Docker Hub or GitHub Container Registry. You push images to it and pull them from it.
A response header listing where a page may load scripts, images, and other resources from, so injected scripts are blocked.
The HTTP header that says what format a body is in, such as application/json.
Passing the trace ID and current span ID along with each outgoing call or message, so the next service joins the same trace.
A small piece of text a server asks the browser to store and send back automatically with later requests to that site.
Copying a shared file only at the moment something changes it, so unchanged files are never duplicated.
One ID attached to every request, log line, and event caused by the same user action, so they can be traced across services.
Cross-Origin Resource Sharing: the rules a browser follows before letting a page read responses from a different origin, and the headers a server sends to allow it.
An index that contains every column a query needs, so the database can answer from the index alone without reading the table.
Work that keeps the processor busy calculating, such as hashing a password or resizing an image, rather than waiting.
Trying email and password pairs leaked from one site on another site, hoping people reused their passwords.
The evidence you present to prove who you are, such as a password, a one-time code, or a passkey.
The standard Linux tool that runs commands automatically on a schedule, like every night at 02:30.
Five fields (minute, hour, day of month, month, day of week) that describe when a scheduled job runs, for example 30 2 * * * for 02:30 every day.
A cron table: the list of scheduled commands for a user, edited with crontab -e.
A request sent to a certificate authority containing your public key and domain name, asking it to sign a certificate.
Cross-site request forgery: another website makes the user's browser send a request to your site, with the user's cookies attached.
Paging through a list by asking for the next N items after the last one seen, which stays fast and stable on deep pages.
A program that runs in the background, waiting for work, such as sshd waiting for SSH logins.
A program that stores data safely on disk and lets you search and change it, for example PostgreSQL or MongoDB.
An open, logged-in channel between your app and the database. Opening one costs network round trips, authentication, and server memory.
A rule the database enforces on every write, such as NOT NULL, UNIQUE, CHECK (stock >= 0), or a foreign key.
The low-level library that sends SQL text to a database and returns rows, such as pg for PostgreSQL in Node.js.
A versioned script, kept in the repo, that changes the database's structure. A tool records which migrations each database has already run.
One self-contained UDP message. It is sent with no connection, no ordering, and no confirmation that it arrived.
A Node.js library that collects many single lookups made during one tick of the event loop and runs them as one batched query.
An attack that floods a service with traffic from many machines at once so real users can't reach it.
A separate holding area for messages or jobs that failed too many times or failed permanently, kept for people to inspect, fix, and replay.
Two transactions each wait for a lock the other holds, so neither can continue. PostgreSQL detects it and aborts one of them.
Deliberately storing a copy or precomputed value to make an important read faster, while taking on the job of keeping it in sync.
Treating every action as forbidden unless a rule explicitly allows it, so a forgotten check blocks access instead of leaking data.
A Kubernetes object that manages ReplicaSets and performs rolling updates and rollbacks.
npm packages needed only to build or test an app, such as TypeScript or a test runner, and not to run it.
Reading another transaction's change before it commits. If it rolls back, you acted on data that never existed. PostgreSQL never allows it.
A lock stored in a shared place, such as Redis, that several servers respect, so only one of them does a piece of work at a time.
Recording one request's path across several services as a tree of timed steps (spans), so you can see where time went.
Domain Name System: the internet's phone book. It turns a name like example.com into the IP address of a server.
The delay before everyone sees a changed DNS record. Nothing is actually pushed out: old answers stay in caches until their TTL expires.
One entry in a domain's DNS settings: a name, a type (such as A or MX), a value, and a TTL.
The server that looks up domain names for you, usually run by your internet provider or a public service like 1.1.1.1.
A domain check where you prove control by creating a specific TXT record in DNS. Required for wildcard certificates.
A tool that builds and runs containers, so an app runs the same way on a laptop and on a server.
A tool that defines and runs a multi-container app from one YAML file, with one command.
A read-only template with an app and its dependencies. Running an image creates a container.
Storage managed by Docker that lives outside a container, so its data survives when the container is deleted.
A text file of instructions, one per line, that Docker follows to build an image.
A NoSQL database that stores each record as a JSON-like document, often with related data nested inside. MongoDB is the best-known example.
A human-friendly name for a website, like example.com, that DNS maps to an IP address.
A company that sells and registers domain names for you.
Time when users cannot use an app.
Writing the same change to two systems (like a database and a message broker) as separate steps, where one can succeed while the other fails.
The error a program gets when it tries to listen on an IP and port that another process is already listening on.
Telling the ORM up front which related data you need, so it fetches it in bulk instead of one row at a time.
Amazon's virtual machine service: rent a server by the second and manage everything from the OS up.
A CDN server located in a city near users. It keeps cached copies so requests don't have to travel to your origin server.
Data sent out of a data centre or cloud provider to the internet. Cloud providers usually charge for it.
Scrambling data so only someone with the right key can turn it back into readable form.
One specific URL plus method that an API answers, such as GET /products/42.
A named setting given to a program from outside its code, often used for passwords and configuration.
A temporary port number the operating system picks for the client side of a connection, so replies can find their way back.
The amount of failure an SLO allows, such as 0.1% of requests. Teams slow down risky changes when it is being used up.
An Express middleware with four parameters (err, req, res, next) that Express calls only when an error occurs. Register it last.
Converting special characters so they are shown as text instead of being interpreted, for example turning < into < in HTML.
A version tag a server attaches to a response. The browser sends it back later, and if nothing changed the server answers 304 Not Modified with no body.
A Node.js object that calls the functions you registered whenever a named event happens, such as 'data' or 'close'.
The mechanism in JavaScript that runs one piece of code at a time and picks up the next task when the current one finishes.
How late Node.js timers fire compared to when they should. High delay means CPU-heavy code is blocking the event loop.
Storing the full list of events as the source of truth for an entity and computing its current state by replaying them, like a bank ledger.
A design where services publish events about what happened, and other services react on their own, instead of calling each other directly.
Different parts of a system may briefly disagree after a change, but they all reach the correct state shortly afterwards if no new changes arrive.
To automatically delete entries from a cache to make room for new ones.
The ideal where each message has its effect exactly one time. In practice it is achieved with at-least-once delivery plus idempotent consumers.
The number a program returns when it finishes. 0 means success; anything else means some kind of failure.
The exit code of a process killed with SIGKILL (128 + 9). In containers it often means the memory limit was exceeded.
Making a breaking schema change in safe steps: add the new structure, move code and data over, then remove the old structure once nothing uses it.
A PostgreSQL command that shows the plan for a query. EXPLAIN shows estimates; EXPLAIN ANALYZE also runs it and shows real times and row counts.
Waiting longer after each failed attempt before retrying, typically doubling the wait each time (1 s, 2 s, 4 s...), usually with a maximum cap.
The most widely used web framework for Node.js. It routes requests to your functions and runs them through middleware.
Promoting a replica to become the new primary when the current primary fails, so the app can keep writing.
A runtime setting that turns a feature on or off without a deploy.
A number the operating system gives a program for each open file or network connection. There is a limit, so leaked ones eventually cause errors.
The read, write, and execute rights on a file, set separately for its owner, its group, and everyone else.
A short summary of a key, used to check quickly that two keys are the same.
A filter that decides which network traffic is allowed in or out of a machine, usually by port and address.
Resolving a bad release by deploying a new fix instead of rolling back to the previous version.
A rate limiting algorithm that counts requests per clock period, like per minute, and resets the count when the period ends.
A chart of profiler results where each bar is a function and wider bars mean more CPU time.
TCP's way of stopping a fast sender from overwhelming a slow receiver: the receiver keeps saying how much more data it has room for.
A column that holds another table's primary key, such as orders.user_id. The database refuses values that don't point to an existing row.
A server that makes requests on behalf of clients, so websites see the proxy instead of the user. The opposite of a reverse proxy.
A property of TLS key exchange: because each connection uses temporary keys, a server key stolen later can't decrypt traffic recorded in the past.
Google SRE's core service metrics: latency, traffic, errors, and saturation.
The part of an app the user sees and interacts with, running in the browser or on the phone.
Both sides of a connection can send data at the same time, independently.
The unique ID of a Git commit, such as 7f3c2a1. Often used to tag images so you know exactly what code is running.
GitHub's built-in CI/CD service. Workflows contain jobs, jobs run steps, and each job runs on a fresh runner.
A fresh virtual machine that runs one GitHub Actions job and is thrown away afterwards.
In GitHub Actions, a YAML file in .github/workflows that says when to run and which jobs to run.
Stopping an app cleanly: stop accepting new requests, finish the ones in progress, close connections, then exit.
An open-source tool for building dashboards and graphs from monitoring data such as Prometheus metrics.
A database that stores items as nodes and the relationships between them as links, suited to questions like "friends of friends". Neo4j is an example.
A query language for APIs where the client asks one endpoint for exactly the fields it needs, described by a typed schema.
An RPC framework where services are defined in .proto files, messages are encoded with Protocol Buffers, and calls run over HTTP/2.
A variant of the gRPC protocol that browsers can use, usually translated to real gRPC by a proxy such as Envoy.
A short exchange of messages two programs do before real work starts, to agree on how they will talk.
A one-way calculation that turns input into a fixed-length fingerprint. You cannot reverse it to get the input back.
Ways a database combines two tables. A hash join builds an in-memory lookup of one side; a nested loop looks up matches for each row, one at a time.
Hypermedia as the engine of application state: API responses include links to related actions, so clients follow links instead of hard-coding URLs.
Deciding at the start of a request whether to record its trace, for example keeping 10%. Cheap, but may drop rare errors.
When one delayed or lost item holds up everything queued behind it, like one lost TCP packet stalling every HTTP/2 request on the connection.
A name and value sent with an HTTP request or response that carries extra information, like Content-Type: application/json.
A computer with no screen, keyboard, or mouse attached. You control it remotely, usually over SSH.
A command or request run regularly to test whether an app really works, not just whether its process is running.
An Express middleware package that sets a group of recommended security headers in one line.
The buffer size limit of a Node.js stream. When it is reached, write() returns false and the source should wait for a 'drain' event.
The share of cache lookups that find the data: hits divided by all lookups.
A video streaming format that splits a video into small segment files plus a playlist file listing them, so it can be served by ordinary web servers and CDNs.
A hash mixed with a secret key, so only someone who knows the key can produce or check the result.
The key a server uses to prove its own identity to SSH clients.
One shard that receives far more traffic than the others, usually because of a poor shard key.
A response header telling the browser to use only HTTPS for a site, for a set time.
Hypertext Transfer Protocol: the request-and-response language browsers and servers use to exchange web pages and data.
Headers sent after the response body. gRPC uses them to report the call's final status.
A domain check where the certificate authority fetches a token file from your server over port 80 to confirm you control the domain.
The 2015 version of HTTP. It splits messages into binary frames and multiplexes many requests over one TCP connection, with header compression.
The 2022 version of HTTP. It runs over QUIC on UDP, so a lost packet only delays its own request and new connections need one round trip.
A cookie attribute that hides the cookie from page JavaScript (document.cookie), so an injected script can't steal it.
HTTP sent inside an encrypted TLS connection, so nobody in between can read or change it.
Software that splits one physical computer into several virtual machines, each with its own share of CPU, memory, and disk.
Input/output: any work where a program asks something outside itself, such as a disk, a database, or the network, and waits for the reply.
Work that spends most of its time waiting for something outside the program, such as a database query or a network call.
In AWS, a set of permissions given to a server or service, so it gets short-lived credentials instead of stored passwords.
A signed JWT from OpenID Connect that tells your app who the user is and which app it was issued for.
A unique id the client creates for one action and sends with every retry, so the server can return the first result instead of doing the work again.
Doing it twice has the same effect as doing it once. Deleting order 42 twice still leaves order 42 deleted.
A bug where changing an ID in a request, like /orders/5002, reveals someone else's data because the server doesn't check ownership.
A SHA-256 fingerprint calculated from an image's or layer's content. The same content always has the same digest.
One slice of a Docker image: the files added, changed, or deleted by one Dockerfile instruction. Layers are shared between images and cached.
A human-friendly name for one version of a Docker image, such as shop-api:1.4.0. Tags can be moved, unlike digests.
A cache kept inside one running copy of your app, for example a JavaScript Map. Fast, but each server has its own copy and it's lost on restart.
An extra sorted structure a database keeps so it can find matching rows without reading the whole table.
A slot Linux uses to track each file. A disk can run out of inodes, and refuse new files, while it still has free space.
A certificate that links a site's certificate to a trusted root CA. Servers must send it along with their own certificate.
A number that identifies a machine on a network, like 203.0.113.10, so data knows where to go.
The original IP address format: four numbers from 0 to 255, like 203.0.113.10. It allows about 4.3 billion addresses.
The newer, much longer IP address format, written in hexadecimal like 2001:db8::1, with enough addresses for practically every device.
A setting that decides how much concurrent transactions can see of each other's changes: read committed, repeatable read, or serializable.
A JavaScript object that stands for a result that isn't ready yet. It is pending, then becomes fulfilled with a value or rejected with an error, exactly once.
Randomness added to wait times or expiry times so that many clients or keys don't all act at the same moment.
The command for reading the journal, the log store where systemd keeps output from services and the kernel.
JavaScript Object Notation: a plain-text format for structured data, like {"id": 42, "name": "Mug"}.
A PostgreSQL column type that stores JSON in a parsed binary form, so you can query and index fields inside it.
A table that links two other tables in a many-to-many relationship, with one row per pair, such as order_items between orders and products.
An encrypted token format, related to JWT, used when the token's contents must be hidden, not just signed.
A JSON document published at a URL that lists an auth server's current public keys, so APIs can verify its tokens.
JSON Web Token: a signed piece of text that carries claims about a user, so a server can check it without looking anything up.
One statement inside a token, such as the user ID (sub) or the expiry time (exp).
A distributed log for event streams. Events are kept for a retention period, split into partitions, and many consumer groups can read and replay them.
The position number of an event in a Kafka partition. Consumer groups store the offset they've reached, like a bookmark.
One ordered, append-only slice of a Kafka topic. Order is guaranteed only within a partition, and each partition is read by one consumer per group.
The core of the operating system. It controls the hardware, runs processes, checks permissions, and handles networking.
Math that lets two sides create the same secret key without ever sending it over the network.
Two linked keys made together: a private key you keep secret, and a public key you can share. What one signs, the other can verify.
Replacing a signing or encryption key with a new one on a schedule, while old tokens or data signed with the previous key are phased out.
A database that stores values under names (keys), like a giant dictionary or JavaScript object.
The most widely used container orchestrator. You declare the desired state and it keeps the cluster matching it.
A group of machines managed together, for example by Kubernetes.
The smallest unit Kubernetes runs: one or more containers that share an IP address. Pods are replaced, not repaired.
A stable name and virtual IP in front of a changing set of pods, which it selects by label.
Amazon's serverless functions: code that runs when an event arrives, billed per request and run time.
How long one request takes from start to finish, usually measured in milliseconds.
Load balancing that understands individual HTTP requests and can spread them across servers, even when they share one connection.
Fetching related data only when code first touches it, such as order.user. Convenient, but each access can be a hidden extra query.
Giving every user and program only the access it needs, so a mistake or break-in does as little damage as possible.
A composite index helps a query only if the query uses its first column (or first few columns). An index on (user_id, created_at) can't search created_at alone.
A free, automated certificate authority that issues the HTTPS certificates used by a large share of websites.
The C library inside Node.js that provides the event loop, talks to the operating system for network I/O, and runs a small thread pool.
A free, open-source operating system that runs most servers on the internet. Ubuntu is one popular version (distribution) of it.
Requests in progress = throughput × latency. At 200 requests per second taking 0.05 s each, about 10 are in progress at once.
Roughly, the average number of processes running or waiting to run. Compared with the number of CPU cores, it shows whether work is queuing.
A server that spreads incoming requests across several app servers so no single one gets overwhelmed.
Sending many requests to a system on purpose to measure its latency and throughput under pressure, usually against a copy of production.
A name that always means "this same machine". It points to the address 127.0.0.1.
Browser storage for strings, per origin, that lasts until deleted. Only page JavaScript can read it, and it is never sent to the server automatically.
A section inside an Nginx server block that matches URL paths and says how to handle them, such as serving files or forwarding to an app.
A PostgreSQL setting that makes a statement give up if it can't get its lock within the given time, instead of waiting and blocking queries behind it.
A label for how serious a log line is, such as debug, info, warn, error, or fatal. Lines below the configured minimum level are dropped.
Regularly renaming, compressing, and deleting old log files so they don't fill the disk.
A small agent, such as Fluent Bit, that copies log lines from servers to a central log store.
A backup that exports data as SQL or a compressed archive, such as with pg_dump. Portable and table-by-table, but slow to restore for large databases.
The client sends a request that the server holds open until there is news or a timeout, then the client asks again.
The special address (127.0.0.1 or ::1) that a computer uses to talk to itself. Traffic sent there never leaves the machine.
Two transactions read the same value and write back a new value computed from it, so one write silently overwrites the other.
The first few bytes of a file that reveal its real format, regardless of its name or claimed type.
A login link with a single-use secret token, emailed to the user, that logs them in when clicked.
An attack where someone secretly sits between two parties, reading or changing what they send.
A relationship where rows on both sides can link to many rows on the other, such as orders and products. It needs a junction table.
A vulnerability where an attacker adds unexpected fields, like isAdmin or price, to a request, and the server saves them because it copies the whole body.
A saved query result that the database stores like a table and refreshes when told to. Fast to read, but can be stale.
The PostgreSQL setting for the most client connections the server accepts at once (100 by default). Past it, new connections are refused.
The computer's fast, temporary working storage. Much faster than disk, but smaller and cleared on restart.
A consumer's confirmation to the broker that a message was handled, so it can be deleted. Without it, the broker redelivers the message.
A server that stores messages from producers and hands them out to consumers, such as RabbitMQ, Kafka, Amazon SQS, or Redis.
An architecture where an app is split into separate small services, each with its own code and usually its own database, talking over the network.
A small job, such as a promise's .then callback or the code after an await, that runs as soon as the current code finishes, before timers or new I/O.
A function that runs in the middle of handling a request, for example to check login or parse the body, before the final handler.
A browser guessing a file's type from its contents instead of trusting the Content-Type header.
Requiring two or more different kinds of evidence to log in, such as a password plus a code from your phone.
A Dockerfile with several FROM stages, where a later stage copies only the finished output from an earlier one, so build tools stay out of the final image.
The format browsers use to send form fields and files in one request body, with parts separated by a boundary string.
Sending many requests and responses at the same time over one connection by interleaving their pieces, as HTTP/2 and HTTP/3 do.
How PostgreSQL handles concurrent access: updates write new row versions, and each transaction reads a consistent snapshot, so readers and writers don't block each other.
A DNS record that says which mail servers receive email for a domain, each with a priority number (lower is tried first).
Running one query to get a list of N items, then one more query per item, instead of fetching the related data in one batch.
A Linux kernel feature that limits what a process can see, such as other processes, network interfaces, or files. Containers are built from them.
Network Address Translation: a router shares one public IP address among many devices by rewriting outgoing traffic and remembering where each reply belongs.
A real-world value that is already unique, like an email address or ISBN. Usually kept UNIQUE rather than used as the primary key.
One connection point between a computer and a network, such as a Wi-Fi card, an Ethernet port, or the loopback interface. Each has its own IP address.
A fast web server often placed in front of apps to handle HTTPS, serve files, and forward requests.
Node's built-in type for a fixed-size block of raw bytes, used for binary data such as file contents and network packets.
An object that hands data over in small chunks as it arrives, instead of all at once, so large data needs little memory.
Reading the same row twice in one transaction and getting different values, because another transaction committed a change in between.
A level of normalization. Third normal form means every column depends on the key, the whole key, and nothing but the key.
Organizing tables so each fact is stored in exactly one place, which prevents copies from contradicting each other.
"Not only SQL": a loose name for databases that don't use tables and joins, such as document, key-value, wide-column, and graph databases.
An npm command that installs exactly the versions in package-lock.json and fails if they don't match package.json. Made for automated builds.
A DNS record that names the authoritative nameservers for a domain.
A standard that lets an app get limited, revocable access to a user's data on another service without seeing their password.
In OAuth, one named permission an app asks for, such as email or permission to upload videos.
A storage service, like Amazon S3, that keeps files (objects) by name inside buckets. Cheap, durable, and built for huge files.
MongoDB's default 12-byte document id: a creation timestamp, a per-process random value, and a counter. Unique without asking the server and roughly ordered by time.
Writing file permissions as three digits, like 755 or 644, where read = 4, write = 2, execute = 1 are added up for owner, group, and others.
Object-document mapper: the MongoDB version of an ORM, such as Mongoose, which adds schemas and validation in your code.
Paging through a list by skipping a number of rows (offset) and taking the next N. Simple, but slow on deep pages and unstable when rows are added.
A foreign key option that automatically deletes child rows when their parent row is deleted, such as an order's items when the order is deleted.
Being the engineer responsible for responding to production alerts, including outside working hours, for a set period.
A relationship where one row is linked to many rows in another table, such as one user with many orders. The foreign key goes on the "many" side.
The part of the Linux kernel that ends a process, usually the largest, when the machine runs out of memory.
A layer on top of OAuth 2.0 for login. It gives the app a signed ID token saying who the user is.
A vendor-neutral open standard and set of libraries for producing traces, metrics, and logs, which can send data to many backends.
The base software that runs a computer, such as Ubuntu or Windows, and lets other programs use its hardware.
An expected failure you can explain to the client, such as invalid input, a missing record, or a declined card.
Optimistic: don't lock, but check a version number at write time and retry on conflict. Pessimistic: lock the rows first so others wait.
A system that places, connects, heals, and updates containers across many machines, such as Kubernetes.
The scheme, host, and port of a URL together, like https://shop.example.com:443. Browsers use it to decide what a page may access.
Object-relational mapper: a library that maps database tables to objects in your code and turns method calls into SQL, such as Prisma, Drizzle, or Sequelize.
Downloading more data than a screen needs, because an endpoint returns a fixed, larger shape.
A non-profit community that publishes free web security guidance, including the Top 10 list of the most common web app weaknesses.
A hosting service that runs your code for you. The provider manages the servers, operating system, and restarts; you just deploy.
A tool that downloads, installs, and updates software for you. Ubuntu's is apt.
A small chunk of data, typically up to about 1,500 bytes, that travels across a network on its own. Larger messages are split into many packets.
A database query where values are sent separately from the SQL text, so input can never be run as SQL.
An index over only the rows that match a condition, such as videos still processing. Smaller and cheaper to maintain.
A login credential made of a key pair stored on your device. The site keeps only the public key, and the device signs a challenge after you unlock it.
One secret value for the whole app, kept outside the database and mixed into password hashing as extra protection.
A way to describe latency across many requests. p95 is the time 95% of requests beat; p99 shows the slowest 1%. Averages hide these slow requests.
Pre-registered GraphQL queries the client refers to by a hash, which makes them cacheable and blocks arbitrary queries.
PostgreSQL's tool for logical backups of one database. pg_restore loads its custom-format archives back in.
A PostgreSQL system view listing every connection and the query it is currently running, with timing and wait information.
A PostgreSQL extension that records how often each query shape runs and how long it takes, used to find the most expensive queries.
A lightweight connection pooler that sits in front of PostgreSQL and lets thousands of client connections share a few real database connections.
Running the same query twice in one transaction and seeing new rows appear, because another transaction inserted matching rows.
Tricking someone into entering their login details on a fake site or form that looks real.
A login method that cannot be used on a fake site even if the user is fooled, such as a passkey that only works on the real domain.
A copy of the database server's raw data files, such as with pg_basebackup. Restores quickly but only onto the same PostgreSQL major version.
The unique number Linux gives each running process. You use it to inspect or signal that process.
The first process in a container (or system). Linux does not apply default signal actions to it, so it must handle SIGTERM itself.
An OAuth add-on where the app proves it started the login with a secret verifier, making stolen authorization codes useless.
A process manager for Node.js apps, with extras such as cluster mode and zero-downtime reloads.
Restoring a base backup and replaying archived WAL up to a chosen moment, such as the minute before an accidental DELETE.
A message that fails every time it is processed, for example because its data is invalid. Without a retry limit it loops forever.
The client asking the server on a timer whether anything has changed.
Using several kinds of databases in one system, each for what it does best, such as PostgreSQL for orders and Redis for sessions.
A number from 0 to 65535 that says which program on a machine should receive network traffic, like an apartment number on a building.
A write-up after an incident: timeline, impact, root cause, and action items. Blameless ones focus on how the system allowed the failure, not on who.
An OPTIONS request the browser sends before certain cross-origin requests, to ask the server whether that origin, method, and headers are allowed.
A storage URL with a signature that allows one specific action, such as uploading one file, until it expires, without sharing your credentials.
The column (or columns) that uniquely identifies each row in a table. It can never be empty or repeated.
A cache that stores responses for one user only, such as the browser's cache.
An address reserved for local networks (10.x.x.x, 172.16-31.x.x, 192.168.x.x). It works inside a network but is never routed on the public internet.
The secret half of a key pair. It proves your identity and must never leave your device.
A port number below 1024. On Linux, only root (or a program given special permission) can listen on one.
A standard JSON format for API errors, with fields like type, title, status, and detail.
A program that is currently running, with its own memory and an ID number the operating system gives it.
A program that starts your app, restarts it when it crashes, and collects its logs, such as systemd, PM2, or Docker.
A Node.js function that schedules a callback to run right after the current operation, even before promise callbacks.
A tool that samples which code the CPU is running, showing which functions use the most time.
A bug in the code, such as reading a property of undefined. The client gets a generic 500 and developers fix the code.
An open-source monitoring system that regularly fetches (scrapes) numbers from apps, stores them as time series, and evaluates alert rules.
An agreed set of rules for how two programs exchange messages.
A language for describing data structures plus a compact binary format that sends numbered fields instead of field names.
The Nginx setting that forwards a request to another server, such as a Node app on 127.0.0.1:3000.
A messaging pattern where senders publish messages to a channel and every subscriber of that channel receives them, without knowing about each other.
An address that is unique worldwide and reachable across the internet.
The shareable half of a key pair. Servers store it to recognise you.
Telling Docker to forward traffic from a host port to a container port, such as -p 8080:3000. On Linux, published ports bypass ufw.
A request to merge a branch into another, usually main, where teammates review the change and CI runs.
A request sent to a database to read or change data, for example a SQL SELECT statement.
A library whose functions mirror SQL clauses (select, from, where) and build safe, parameterized SQL for you, such as Knex or Kysely.
The part of the database that decides how to run a query, such as which index to use and how to join tables, based on cost estimates.
The part of a URL after the ?, holding extra parameters such as ?category=audio&limit=20.
A waiting line for work: one program adds jobs, another takes them out and processes them in turn.
A transport protocol built on UDP that adds reliability per stream and builds TLS 1.3 into its handshake. HTTP/3 runs on it.
A message broker where producers publish to exchanges that route messages into queues; messages are deleted once acknowledged.
The part of RabbitMQ that receives published messages and routes them to queues according to bindings and the message's routing key.
A bug where the result depends on the exact timing of overlapping operations, such as two requests both buying the last item.
A huge precomputed list of hashes and the passwords that produce them. Salts make these useless.
An HTTP request for only part of a file, which lets a video player jump to the middle without downloading the start.
Capping how many requests a client can make in a period of time, and rejecting the rest.
Amazon's managed relational database service, which handles patching, backups, and failover for you.
A copy of the database that receives every change from the primary (the one server that takes writes) and serves reads only.
Kubernetes health checks: readiness decides if a pod gets traffic; liveness decides if a stuck pod is restarted.
A checklist for monitoring anything that serves requests: Rate (requests per second), Errors, and Duration.
A response telling the browser to go to a different URL instead, for example from http:// to https://.
The exact URL, registered in advance, where an OAuth provider sends the user back after login.
An in-memory data store that is very fast, often used for caching, sessions, counters, and simple queues.
A Redis data type that works as an append-only log of messages, with consumer groups and acknowledgments, so messages aren't lost if a consumer crashes.
Regular expression denial of service: input crafted so a badly written regex takes a very long time, blocking the server.
A longer-lived token used only to get new access tokens. The server tracks it, so it can be revoked.
A database that stores data in tables of rows and columns and links tables through ids, queried with SQL. PostgreSQL and MySQL are examples.
A file location written from the folder you are currently in, like logs/app.log.
Turning HTML, CSS, and data into the pixels you see on screen.
The delay between a write committing on the primary and it appearing on a replica. During lag, reads from the replica return old data.
A group of MongoDB servers holding copies of the same data: one primary that takes writes and secondaries that follow it and can take over.
A Kubernetes object that keeps a set number of identical pods running.
Keeping copies of the same database on several servers, so reads can be spread out and a copy can take over if the main server fails.
A message a client sends to a server asking for something, such as a page or some data.
Letting many simultaneous requests for the same data share one in-progress load instead of each starting their own.
The first line of an HTTP request: the method, the path, and the protocol version, like POST /orders HTTP/1.1.
The message a server sends back to answer a request, with a status code, headers, and usually a body.
Representational State Transfer: an API style where URLs name resources and standard HTTP methods and status codes act on them.
A Docker setting, like unless-stopped, that tells Docker when to restart a container automatically.
Sending data again because the receiver didn't confirm it arrived. TCP does this automatically.
A response header telling the client how many seconds to wait before trying again.
A server that receives requests from the internet and forwards them to app servers behind it.
Giving permissions to roles like seller or admin, and giving roles to users, instead of granting permissions person by person.
Returning to the previous version of an app after a bad release.
Updating servers to a new version a few at a time, so old and new code run side by side for a while and the site never goes fully down.
The underlying reason a problem happened, as opposed to its symptom. For example 'the endpoint was not idempotent', not 'orders were duplicated'.
The top folder of a Linux system, written /. Every file and folder on the machine sits somewhere below it.
The servers at the top of DNS. They don't know any domain's address, but they know where to find the servers for each top-level domain like .com.
The administrator account on Linux (user ID 0). It can read and change any file and run anything.
One message travelling to the other side plus the reply coming back. Many network steps cost one round trip each.
A named part of a URL pattern, like :id in /orders/:id, whose value Express puts in req.params.
A label on a RabbitMQ message, like order.placed.eu, that exchanges use to decide which queues get it.
Calling a function that runs on another machine as if it were a normal local function call.
Recovery point objective: how much recent data you can afford to lose in a disaster, measured in time.
The amount of physical memory (RAM) a process is actually using right now.
A file copying tool that compares source and destination and sends only what changed. It works locally or over SSH.
Recovery time objective: how long you can afford to be down while restoring from a failure.
Amazon's object storage: files stored in buckets under keys, read and written over HTTPS.
Uploading one large file to S3 as separate parts that can go in parallel and be retried alone, then joined into one object.
An HTTP method that must not change anything on the server, such as GET, HEAD, or OPTIONS.
A multi-step process across services where each step is its own transaction and has an undo step that runs if a later step fails.
A random value, different for each user, mixed into a password before hashing so identical passwords produce different hashes.
The browser rule that a page's JavaScript may not read responses from a different origin unless that server allows it with CORS headers.
A cookie attribute (Strict, Lax, or None) that controls whether the browser sends the cookie on requests started by other sites. Lax and Strict help block CSRF.
A named checkpoint inside a transaction that you can roll back to without abandoning the whole transaction.
Running a query on every shard and combining the results, needed when the query doesn't filter on the shard key. Slower than a single-shard query.
The declared structure of a database: which tables exist, their columns, and each column's type and rules.
Checking incoming data against a written description of the allowed fields, types, and limits before using it.
The database stores data in any shape, and your code interprets the structure when it reads it. Typical of document databases.
The database checks data against a declared structure when you save it, and rejects data that doesn't fit. Typical of relational databases.
A command that copies files to or from a server over SSH.
Replacing a password or API key with a new one and revoking the old one, routinely or after a leak.
A service that stores passwords and API keys securely, controls who can read them, logs access, and can rotate them.
A cloud provider's firewall that filters traffic before it reaches your virtual machine. By default it blocks all incoming traffic.
A query that locks the rows it reads, so other transactions trying to change or lock them must wait until this one finishes.
How small a share of rows a condition matches. A highly selective condition (one user's orders) benefits most from an index.
The position number TCP gives each byte it sends, so the receiver can put data back in order and spot gaps.
Reading every row of a table to find the matching ones. Fine for small tables, slow for finding a few rows in a big one.
An error (code 40001) where the database aborts a transaction that conflicted with a concurrent one. The app should retry it.
A computer, or a program on it, that waits for requests and sends back responses.
A section of Nginx config that describes one website, chosen by port and domain name (server_name).
A web standard where the server keeps one HTTP response open and pushes text events to the browser, which reconnects automatically.
Code the cloud provider starts on demand and scales automatically, such as AWS Lambda. Each running instance is a separate process.
Data a server keeps about a logged-in user between requests, usually found through an ID stored in a cookie.
An attack where the attacker makes the victim use a session ID the attacker already knows, so it becomes a logged-in session after the victim logs in.
A long random value that identifies one server-side session. The browser holds it in a cookie; the user's data stays on the server.
Like localStorage, but each tab has its own copy and it is cleared when the tab closes.
A special permission that makes a program run as the file's owner instead of the user who started it. /usr/bin/passwd uses it.
The column, such as user_id, that decides which shard a row is stored on. It should have many values, spread load evenly, and appear in most queries.
Splitting one dataset across several database servers, each holding part of the rows, so no single machine has to store or serve all of it.
The area of memory where PostgreSQL keeps recently used data pages so repeated reads don't have to go to disk. It caches pages, not query results.
A cache that stores one copy of a response and serves it to many users, such as a CDN or reverse proxy. Personal data must never be stored in one.
The program that reads the commands you type in a terminal and runs them. On Ubuntu it is usually bash.
The forced stop signal (number 9). The kernel ends the process immediately; it can't be caught, so nothing is cleaned up.
The polite stop signal (number 15). A program can catch it, finish its work, clean up, and exit.
An attack where someone convinces a mobile carrier to move your phone number to their SIM card, so they receive your text messages and SMS codes.
A layered linked list that allows fast searching in sorted order. Redis uses one inside sorted sets.
A measured number describing service quality, such as the share of requests that succeed in under 1 second.
A target for a measured service quality, such as 99.9% of checkout requests succeeding over 30 days.
Server Name Indication: the field in the TLS handshake where the browser names the site it wants, so one server can host many HTTPS sites.
A real-time library built on WebSockets that adds rooms, reconnection, and fallbacks, using its own protocol on top.
A general relay that forwards any kind of network traffic for an app. ssh -D turns an SSH connection into one.
A Redis data type holding unique members, each with a numeric score, always kept in score order. Used for leaderboards and sliding-window rate limits.
The one place whose data is considered correct when copies disagree, usually the main database.
Structured Query Language: the language used to read and change data in relational databases like PostgreSQL.
An attack where user input is pasted into a SQL query and changes what the query does, for example reading every user's data.
Secure Shell: an encrypted way to log in to and run commands on a remote machine.
Sending another program's network traffic through an encrypted SSH connection, for example to reach a private database from your laptop.
An attack that makes your server fetch a URL the attacker chooses, often an internal address the attacker can't reach directly.
The list of function calls that led to an error, with file names and line numbers, showing where the error happened.
A Cache-Control directive (and caching strategy) that lets a cache keep serving an expired copy for a short time while it fetches a fresh one in the background.
A separate stream where a program writes error messages, so errors can be kept apart from normal output.
The stream where a program writes its normal results. By default it goes to the screen, but it can be redirected to a file or piped to another program.
A shape for behavioral answers: Situation, Task, Action, Result, with most time spent on the Action.
A Kubernetes check that gives a slow-starting app time to boot before liveness checks begin.
A firewall that remembers open connections, so replies to traffic your server started are let back in automatically.
Treating every request on its own, with no memory of earlier ones. Each request must carry everything needed, such as a login cookie.
A three-digit number in an HTTP response that says what happened, like 200 (OK) or 404 (not found).
The first line of an HTTP response: the version, the status code, and a short reason, like HTTP/1.1 201 Created.
A special permission on a folder that lets only a file's owner delete or rename it. /tmp uses it so users can't delete each other's files.
PostgreSQL's built-in replication: the primary streams its write-ahead log (WAL) records to replicas, which replay them to stay in sync.
A log line written as named fields, usually JSON, instead of a free-form sentence, so tools can search and filter by field.
A command that runs one command with administrator (root) rights.
A generated id with no real-world meaning, used as a primary key because it never needs to change.
Encryption that uses one shared secret key to both lock and unlock data. It is fast, so TLS uses it for the actual traffic.
Synchronous: the primary waits for a replica to confirm each commit, so confirmed writes are never lost but writes are slower. Asynchronous (the default): it doesn't wait.
The program that boots Ubuntu and runs as process 1. It starts, stops, restarts, and logs background services.
Splitting one large table into smaller pieces, such as one per month, on the same database server.
Deciding whether to keep a trace after it finishes, so all errors and slow traces can be kept. Needs a collector that buffers spans.
Transmission Control Protocol: delivers data reliably and in order, resending anything that gets lost.
The text window where you type commands.
A single line of execution inside a process. One thread can do exactly one thing at a time.
A small set of helper threads (4 by default in Node.js) that run file system calls, DNS lookups, and some heavy crypto so the main thread stays free.
The three messages (SYN, SYN-ACK, ACK) that open a TCP connection and agree on starting sequence numbers. It costs one round trip.
How much work a system finishes per second, such as requests per second.
A sequence of values of one metric over time, each with a timestamp. It is what a monitoring graph draws.
How long from sending a request until the first byte of the response arrives. Mostly measures how long the server took to start answering.
A short period (60 seconds on Linux) after a TCP connection closes during which the side that closed first still remembers it, so stray old packets are not confused with a new connection.
Transport Layer Security: the encryption layer behind HTTPS. SSL is its older, retired name.
Decrypting HTTPS traffic at a proxy or load balancer, which then forwards plain HTTP to the app behind it.
A mount stored only in memory, which disappears when the container stops.
A rate limiting algorithm where tokens refill at a steady rate and each request spends one, which allows short bursts.
The last part of a domain name, such as .com, .org, or .in. TLD servers know which nameservers are in charge of each domain under them.
A 6-digit login code that an authenticator app computes from a shared secret and the current time, changing every 30 seconds.
A random ID shared by every step of one request across all services, used to group them into one trace.
The W3C standard HTTP header that carries the trace ID, parent span ID, and sampling flag between services.
A group of database changes that either all happen (COMMIT) or none happen (ROLLBACK).
Saving an event row in the same transaction as the data change, then having a worker publish it to other services, so neither can happen without the other.
Converting a video into other sizes and formats (for example 1080p, 720p, 480p) so it plays smoothly on any device.
A temporary failure, like a timeout or a 503, that may succeed if you try again later.
The point where data enters your system from a source you don't control, such as a request body. Everything crossing it must be checked.
The list of root certificate authorities that an operating system or browser trusts out of the box.
Time To Live: how long a saved copy may be used before it counts as expired.
A DNS record holding free text, mostly used to prove domain ownership and to publish email security settings like SPF.
User Datagram Protocol: sends data quickly without checking that it arrived or arrived in order.
Ubuntu's simple firewall tool. You write rules like 'allow port 443' and it configures the kernel's packet filter for you.
The number Linux uses to identify a user account. root is always 0.
A setting that removes permissions from newly created files by default. With the common 022, new files start at 644 and folders at 755.
Needing several requests to build one screen, because no single endpoint returns enough data.
A promise that failed with nobody handling the error. Since Node.js 15, it crashes the process by default.
A filesystem that stacks several folders so they look like one, with higher layers hiding lower ones. Docker uses it to combine image layers.
A small config file that tells systemd how to run a service: the command, the user, restart rules, and when to start it.
A contradiction caused by storing one fact in many rows and changing only some of them, such as a user with two different emails.
An outside service that requests your site regularly from the internet and alerts you when it fails, as a customer would see it.
Uniform Resource Locator: a web address, like https://shop.example.com/products/42.
A checklist for monitoring resources such as CPU, memory, and disk: Utilization, Saturation (queued work), and Errors.
Discovering which usernames or emails have accounts from differences in an app's error messages or response times.
A 128-bit identifier that can be generated anywhere without coordination and is practically never repeated, such as 3f1c9a2e-...
The JavaScript engine, also used by Chrome, that runs your JavaScript code inside Node.js.
PostgreSQL's cleanup process. It removes row versions no transaction can see any more and keeps the table's bookkeeping up to date.
A virtual CPU: the slice of a real processor core given to a virtual machine. On cheaper plans it may be shared with other customers.
A software-made computer running on a real one. It has its own operating system and behaves like a separate machine.
In Amazon SQS, how long a received message stays hidden from other consumers. If it isn't deleted in time, it becomes visible and is redelivered.
Virtual Private Server: a rented slice of a physical machine that behaves like your own server.
A log where PostgreSQL records every change before applying it to the data files. Flushing it at COMMIT is what makes committed data survive a crash.
Copying each finished write-ahead log file to safe storage, so changes since the last base backup can be replayed during recovery.
The browser standard that lets websites create and use passkeys and hardware security keys.
A long-lived connection, started by upgrading an HTTP request, over which client and server can both send messages at any time.
A NoSQL database, such as Cassandra, that groups rows by a partition key and spreads them across many machines, built for very high write volumes.
A certificate that covers every subdomain at one level, like *.example.com.
A setting that controls how slow a password hashing algorithm is, so it can be raised as computers get faster.
A separate program whose only task is to take jobs from a queue and do them.
Extra JavaScript threads in Node.js, each with its own event loop, used to run CPU-heavy work without blocking the main thread.
Two transactions read the same data and each writes something different based on it; together they break a rule neither broke alone.
An HTTP header that proxies add to record the original client's IP address, since the app otherwise sees only the proxy's address.
Cross-site scripting: an attacker gets their own JavaScript to run on your pages, where it can read page data and act as the user.
A text format for configuration files that uses indentation to show structure.
Releasing a new version without users noticing any interruption.
A popular JavaScript and TypeScript library for describing data schemas and validating values against them.
A process that has finished but whose parent hasn't collected its exit code yet. It uses no CPU or memory, only a slot in the process table.
